claim: Higher proportions of potential pathogens were detected in core microbial taxa in leaf litter than rhizosphere soil.
source: We found that higher proportions of potential pathogens were detected in core microbial taxa in leaf litter than rhizosphere soil and thus leaf inoculation had more adverse effects on seed germination and seedling survival than soil inoculation.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3g-h showing the abundance of plant fungal pathogens was greater in leaves (68.20%) than in soil (33.93%), and Figure 3c-d showing plant bacterial pathogens (2.29%) were detected in leaves but not in soil.

claim: Leaf inoculation had more adverse effects on seed germination and seedling survival than soil inoculation.
source: We found that higher proportions of potential pathogens were detected in core microbial taxa in leaf litter than rhizosphere soil and thus leaf inoculation had more adverse effects on seed germination and seedling survival than soil inoculation.
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Figure 1 showing that sterile leaf inoculation significantly delayed germination time (Figure 1a), and non-sterile leaf inoculation at G0 caused 96.7% mortality rate compared to lower rates for soil inoculation (Figure 1c-d).

claim: Microbial inoculation at different growth stages altered the microbial community and functions of seedlings.
source: Microbial inoculation at different growth stages altered the microbial community and functions of seedlings, and earlier inoculation had a more adverse effect on seedling survival and growth.
evidence: The claim is supported by NMDS and PERMANOVA analyses showing that inoculation time significantly affected bacterial and fungal community and functional assembly (Figure 5a-h), with R2 values of 0.102-0.138.

claim: Earlier inoculation had a more adverse effect on seedling survival and growth than later inoculation.
source: Microbial inoculation at different growth stages altered the microbial community and functions of seedlings, and earlier inoculation had a more adverse effect on seedling survival and growth.
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Figure 1d showing that non-sterile leaf inoculation at earlier stages significantly increased seedling mortality compared with later stages, and Figure 2b showing that seedlings inoculated at G0 had poorer growth than those inoculated at later stages.

claim: The soil nutrient level did not affect microbe-mediated seedling growth.
source: The soil nutrient level did not affect microbe-mediated seedling growth and the relative abundance of the microbial community and functions involved in seedling growth.
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Figure 2a showing that nutrition level did not significantly affect the response index (p=0.0681), and Figure 6 showing no difference in the relative abundance of microbes or functions involved in seedling growth under different nutrient levels.

claim: The soil nutrient level did not affect the relative abundance of the microbial community and functions involved in seedling growth.
source: The soil nutrient level did not affect microbe-mediated seedling growth and the relative abundance of the microbial community and functions involved in seedling growth.
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Figure 6a-e showing that there was no difference in the relative abundance of microbes or functions involved in seedling growth under different nutrient levels.

claim: The effects of some microbial genera on seedling survival are distinct from those on growth.
source: The effects of some microbial genera on seedling survival are distinct from those on growth.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing that bacterial genera Pseudomonas, Sphingomonas, and Massilia are positively correlated with seedling mortality (Figure 3i) but also positively correlated with subsequent seedling growth (Figure 6a-b), and fungi Mortierella and Hypocrea are negatively correlated with early seedling mortality (Figure 3j) but positively correlated with later seedling growth (Figure 6a-b).

claim: The A. adenophora seedling-killing effects of fungal strains isolated from dead seedlings by non-sterile leaf inoculation exhibited significant phylogenetic signals.
source: Moreover, the A. adenophora seedling-killing effects of fungal strains isolated from dead seedlings by non-sterile leaf inoculation exhibited significant phylogenetic signals, by which strains of Allophoma and Alternaria generally caused high seedling mortality.
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Figure 4c showing that the seedling-killing effects exhibited a significant phylogenetic signal (Pagel's λ=0.82, p=0.0002).

claim: Strains of Allophoma and Alternaria generally caused high seedling mortality.
source: Moreover, the A. adenophora seedling-killing effects of fungal strains isolated from dead seedlings by non-sterile leaf inoculation exhibited significant phylogenetic signals, by which strains of Allophoma and Alternaria generally caused high seedling mortality.
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Figure 4c showing that numerically dominant Allophoma (Didymellaceae) and Alternaria (Pleosporaceae) had high seedling mortality (54–100%).

claim: PSFs are usually positive for plant invasion because of escaping soil pathogens and recruiting some beneficial microbes.
source: For plant invasion, PSFs are usually positive because of escaping soil pathogens and recruiting some beneficial microbes (Liu et al., 2023; Mitchell and Power, 2003; Xu et al., 2012) or negative effects because of accumulating local pathogens (Callaway et al., 2013; Flory and Clay, 2013; Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research (Liu et al., 2023; Mitchell and Power, 2003; Xu et al., 2012).

claim: PSFs can be negative for plant invasion because of accumulating local pathogens.
source: For plant invasion, PSFs are usually positive because of escaping soil pathogens and recruiting some beneficial microbes (Liu et al., 2023; Mitchell and Power, 2003; Xu et al., 2012) or negative effects because of accumulating local pathogens (Callaway et al., 2013; Flory and Clay, 2013; Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research (Callaway et al., 2013; Flory and Clay, 2013; Zhang et al., 2020).

claim: PSFs can affect species coexistence.
source: PSFs can affect species coexistence (Bever et al., 1997; van der Putten et al., 2013) and local plant community composition and dynamics (Bauer et al., 2017; Kardol et al., 2007; Teste et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research (Bever et al., 1997; van der Putten et al., 2013).

claim: PSFs can affect local plant community composition and dynamics.
source: PSFs can affect species coexistence (Bever et al., 1997; van der Putten et al., 2013) and local plant community composition and dynamics (Bauer et al., 2017; Kardol et al., 2007; Teste et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research (Bauer et al., 2017; Kardol et al., 2007; Teste et al., 2017).

claim: Leaf litter can affect plant growth, species diversity, and community structure.
source: Similar to soil, leaf litter can also affect plant growth, species diversity, and community structure (Liu et al., 2017; Ma et al., 2020; Olson and Wallander, 2002), thus playing important roles in population establishment and community dynamics (Jessen et al., 2023; Lamb, 2008; Xiong and Nilsson, 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research (Liu et al., 2017; Ma et al., 2020; Olson and Wallander, 2002).

claim: Leaf litter plays important roles in population establishment and community dynamics.
source: Similar to soil, leaf litter can also affect plant growth, species diversity, and community structure (Liu et al., 2017; Ma et al., 2020; Olson and Wallander, 2002), thus playing important roles in population establishment and community dynamics (Jessen et al., 2023; Lamb, 2008; Xiong and Nilsson, 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research (Jessen et al., 2023; Lamb, 2008; Xiong and Nilsson, 1999).

claim: All four Asteraceae species experienced stronger negative PPFs than PSFs.
source: Until 2017, Whitaker et al., 2017, extended the PSF to aboveground tissues (including leaf, stem, and ﬂoral tissues), termed 'plant-phyllosphere feedbacks (PPFs)', and found that all four Asteraceae species experienced stronger negative PPFs than PSFs.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Whitaker et al., 2017.

claim: All 10 tested Asteraceae plants experienced negative PPFs.
source: Subsequently, this team further verified that all 10 tested Asteraceae plants experienced negative PPFs (Zaret et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Zaret et al., 2021.

claim: The lack of strong mutualists and relatively high abundance of pathogens in the phyllosphere may account for the negative PPFs.
source: The lack of strong mutualists and relatively high abundance of pathogens in the phyllosphere may account for the negative PPFs.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observed negative PPFs and known characteristics of phyllosphere microbial communities.

claim: Younger seedlings were more susceptible to infection by soil microbes because of fewer defense resources.
source: For example, seedlings showed distinct sensitivity during the growth stage, and younger seedlings were more susceptible to infection by soil microbes because of fewer defense resources (Geisen et al., 2021; Jevon et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research (Geisen et al., 2021; Jevon et al., 2020).

claim: Leaf litter has an adverse effect on seedling emergence but a positive effect on later plant growth.
source: Interestingly, leaf litter has an adverse effect on seedling emergence but a positive effect on later plant growth (Abbas et al., 2023; Möhler et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2022); litter also has a stronger negative effect on earlier vegetation growth than on the elder (Loydi et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2022; Xiong and Nilsson, 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research (Abbas et al., 2023; Möhler et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2022).

claim: Litter has a stronger negative effect on earlier vegetation growth than on the elder.
source: Interestingly, leaf litter has an adverse effect on seedling emergence but a positive effect on later plant growth (Abbas et al., 2023; Möhler et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2022); litter also has a stronger negative effect on earlier vegetation growth than on the elder (Loydi et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2022; Xiong and Nilsson, 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research (Loydi et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2022; Xiong and Nilsson, 1999).

claim: Plants enrich distinct microbes under different nutrient conditions and affect plant performance.
source: Moreover, plants enrich distinct microbes under different nutrient conditions and affect plant performance (Dostál, 2021; Gustafson and Casper, 2004; Widdig et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research (Dostál, 2021; Gustafson and Casper, 2004; Widdig et al., 2020).

claim: The bacterial diversity in duckweed plants was reduced under nutrient-deficient conditions, but the abundance of Firmicutes increased.
source: For example, the bacterial diversity in duckweed plants was reduced under nutrient-deficient conditions, but the abundance of Firmicutes increased (Bunyoo et al., 2022), and members of Firmicutes have been reported to promote plant stress tolerance (Xu et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Bunyoo et al., 2022.

claim: Members of Firmicutes have been reported to promote plant stress tolerance.
source: For example, the bacterial diversity in duckweed plants was reduced under nutrient-deficient conditions, but the abundance of Firmicutes increased (Bunyoo et al., 2022), and members of Firmicutes have been reported to promote plant stress tolerance (Xu et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Xu et al., 2018.

claim: Nutrient additions cause crops to enrich some bacteria and fungi from soil and increase yield.
source: Ai et al., 2018, reported that nutrient additions cause crops to enrich some bacteria and fungi from soil and increase yield.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Ai et al., 2018.

claim: Ageratina adenophora has invaded more than 30 countries and areas, including South Africa, Australia, New Zealand, Hawaii, India, and China.
source: Ageratina adenophora (Sprengel) RM King and H Robinson (Asteraceae), known as Crofton weed or Mexican devil weed, has invaded more than 30 countries and areas, including South Africa, Australia, New Zealand, Hawaii, India, and China (Changjun et al., 2021; Julien and Griffiths, 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research (Changjun et al., 2021; Julien and Griffiths, 1998).

claim: A. adenophora is a perennial weed and can produce high yields of seeds with a high germination rate.
source: It is a perennial weed and can produce high yields of seeds with a high germination rate (GR) (Lu et al., 2006; Parsons, 1992).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research (Lu et al., 2006; Parsons, 1992).

claim: A. adenophora can enrich the beneficial soil microbial community to facilitate invasion.
source: Previous studies have shown that A. adenophora can enrich the beneficial soil microbial community to facilitate invasion (Niu et al., 2007; Zhao et al., 2019); in contrast, A. adenophora leaves harbor diverse fungal pathogens that can cause adverse effects on itself seed germination and growth (Fang et al., 2019a; Fang et al., 2021a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research (Niu et al., 2007; Zhao et al., 2019).

claim: A. adenophora leaves harbor diverse fungal pathogens that can cause adverse effects on itself seed germination and growth.
source: Previous studies have shown that A. adenophora can enrich the beneficial soil microbial community to facilitate invasion (Niu et al., 2007; Zhao et al., 2019); in contrast, A. adenophora leaves harbor diverse fungal pathogens that can cause adverse effects on itself seed germination and growth (Fang et al., 2019a; Fang et al., 2021a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research (Fang et al., 2019a; Fang et al., 2021a).

claim: Sterile leaf inoculation significantly delayed germination time more than did soil and non-sterile leaf inoculation, as well as the control.
source: At the G0 timepoint, sterile leaf inoculation significantly delayed germination time more than did soil and non-sterile leaf inoculation, as well as the control (nothing inoculated) (Figure 1a, p<0.05).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1a with statistical significance p<0.05.

claim: Leaf and soil inoculation had no distinct effects on the germination rate.
source: Leaf and soil inoculation had no distinct effects on the GR (Figure 1b, p>0.05).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1b with p>0.05 indicating no significant difference.

claim: Only non-sterile leaves caused a low percentage of seedling death (8.4%) when the seedlings were inoculated at G21.
source: Only non-sterile leaves caused a low percentage of seedling death (8.4%) when the seedlings were inoculated at G21 (Figure 1c, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1c and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Leaf inoculation caused significantly greater seedling mortality than did soil inoculation two weeks after transplanting.
source: Two weeks after transplanting these seedlings into the cups, leaf inoculation caused significantly greater seedling mortality than did soil inoculation (p<0.001); the non-sterile sample caused greater seedling mortality than did the sterile sample, especially leaf inoculation during the G0 and G21 periods.
evidence: The claim is supported by data with statistical significance p<0.001.

claim: The non-sterile sample caused greater seedling mortality than did the sterile sample, especially leaf inoculation during the G0 and G21 periods.
source: Two weeks after transplanting these seedlings into the cups, leaf inoculation caused significantly greater seedling mortality than did soil inoculation (p<0.001); the non-sterile sample caused greater seedling mortality than did the sterile sample, especially leaf inoculation during the G0 and G21 periods.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing sterile and non-sterile samples.

claim: Non-sterile leaf inoculation at earlier stages significantly increased seedling mortality compared with that at later stages.
source: Moreover, non-sterile leaf inoculation at earlier stages significantly increased seedling mortality compared with that at later stages (Figure 1d, p<0.05).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1d with statistical significance p<0.05.

claim: Seedling mortality did not differ between the high and low nutrient conditions, regardless of leaf or soil inoculation.
source: However, seedling mortality did not differ between the high and low nutrient conditions, regardless of leaf or soil inoculation (Figure 1d, both p>0.05).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1d with p>0.05 indicating no significant difference.

claim: Inoculation source and time, as well as their interaction with nutrient level, significantly affected the microbial role in the total dry biomass of A. adenophora.
source: With the exception of nutrient level, inoculation source and time, as well as their interaction with nutrient level, significantly affected the microbial role in the total dry biomass of A. adenophora (p<0.05, Figure 2a).
evidence: The claim is supported by GLM analysis results shown in Figure 2a with p<0.05.

claim: When inoculated at the G0 timepoint, both soil and leaf microbes had adverse effects on A. adenophora growth.
source: Soil and leaf microbial effects on seedling biomass interacted with soil nutrient level and inoculation time: when inoculated at the G0 timepoint, both soil and leaf microbes had adverse effects on A. adenophora growth, as all seedlings inoculated with non-sterile leaves died, and those inoculated with non-sterile soil grew poorer than those inoculated with sterile soil under both low- and high nutrition conditions
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing all seedlings inoculated with non-sterile leaves died and those with non-sterile soil grew poorer than sterile controls.

claim: When inoculated at the G21 timepoint, both soil and leaf microbes had significantly positive effects only under high nutrition conditions.
source: when inoculated at the G21 timepoint, both soil and leaf microbes had significantly positive effects only under high nutrition conditions
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing positive effects under high nutrition conditions at G21 inoculation.

claim: When inoculated at the G28 timepoint, only soil microbes promoted seedling growth under high nutrition conditions.
source: when inoculated at the G28 timepoint, only soil microbes promoted seedling growth under high nutrition conditions
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing only soil microbes had positive effects at G28 under high nutrition.

claim: When inoculated at the G21+28 timepoint, only leaf microbes had a significantly positive effect on seedling growth under low nutrition conditions.
source: when inoculated at the G21+28 timepoint, only leaf microbes had a significantly positive effect on seedling growth under low nutrition conditions (Figure 2b).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: The microbial diversity and richness were greater in the soil than in the leaf litter.
source: The microbial diversity and richness were greater in the soil than in the leaf litter (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Top three core bacteria were Rhodoplanes (5.65%), Bradyrizhobium (4.80%), and some unclassified Alphaproteobacteria (4.56%) for soil.
source: Top three core bacteria were Rhodoplanes (5.65%), Bradyrizhobium (4.80%), and some unclassified Alphaproteobacteria (4.56%) for soil and Pseudomonas (30.33%), Massilia (17.45%), and Sphingomonas (16.35%) for leaf (Figure 3a and b).
evidence: The claim is supported by microbial community composition data shown in Figure 3a and b.

claim: Top three core bacteria were Pseudomonas (30.33%), Massilia (17.45%), and Sphingomonas (16.35%) for leaf.
source: Top three core bacteria were Rhodoplanes (5.65%), Bradyrizhobium (4.80%), and some unclassified Alphaproteobacteria (4.56%) for soil and Pseudomonas (30.33%), Massilia (17.45%), and Sphingomonas (16.35%) for leaf (Figure 3a and b).
evidence: The claim is supported by microbial community composition data shown in Figure 3a and b.

claim: Top three core fungal genera were Mortierella (7.00%), Inocybe (5.36%), and Neonectria (3.63%) for soil.
source: Top three core fungal genera were Mortierella (7.00%), Inocybe (5.36%), and Neonectria (3.63%) for soil and Didymella (27.30%), Alternaria (8.95%), and Cryptococcus (4.44%) for leaf (Figure 3e and f).
evidence: The claim is supported by fungal community composition data shown in Figure 3e and f.

claim: Top three core fungal genera were Didymella (27.30%), Alternaria (8.95%), and Cryptococcus (4.44%) for leaf.
source: Top three core fungal genera were Mortierella (7.00%), Inocybe (5.36%), and Neonectria (3.63%) for soil and Didymella (27.30%), Alternaria (8.95%), and Cryptococcus (4.44%) for leaf (Figure 3e and f).
evidence: The claim is supported by fungal community composition data shown in Figure 3e and f.

claim: Plant bacterial pathogens (2.29%) were the potential function of the core bacterial taxa in leaves but not in soil.
source: Plant bacterial pathogens (2.29%) were the potential function of the core bacterial taxa in leaves but not in soil; soil had a greater abundance of nitrogen circle-related function (50.98%) than did leaves (17.55%) (Figure 3c and d, Figure 3—source data 1 and 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by functional analysis data shown in Figure 3c and d.

claim: Soil had a greater abundance of nitrogen circle-related function (50.98%) than did leaves (17.55%).
source: Plant bacterial pathogens (2.29%) were the potential function of the core bacterial taxa in leaves but not in soil; soil had a greater abundance of nitrogen circle-related function (50.98%) than did leaves (17.55%) (Figure 3c and d, Figure 3—source data 1 and 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by functional analysis data shown in Figure 3c and d.

claim: The abundance of plant fungal pathogens was greater in leaves (68.20%) than in soil (33.93%).
source: The abundance of plant fungal pathogens was greater in leaves (68.20%) than in soil (33.93%) (Figure 3g and h, Figure 3—source data 3 and 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by fungal functional guild data shown in Figure 3g and h.

claim: The leaf core bacterial genera Pseudomonas, Sphingomonas, Massilia, Variovorax, Aureimonas, and Agrobacterium were positively correlated with MR.
source: Specifically, the leaf core bacterial genera Pseudomonas, Sphingomonas, Massilia, Variovorax, Aureimonas, and Agrobacterium were positively correlated with MR, but the soil core bacteria, including Alphaproteobacteria_unclassified, Rhodoplanes, Vicinamibacteraceae_unclassified, and Pedomicrobium, were negatively correlated with MR (Figure 3a, b, and i).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis data shown in Figure 3i.

claim: The soil core bacteria, including Alphaproteobacteria_unclassified, Rhodoplanes, Vicinamibacteraceae_unclassified, and Pedomicrobium, were negatively correlated with MR.
source: Specifically, the leaf core bacterial genera Pseudomonas, Sphingomonas, Massilia, Variovorax, Aureimonas, and Agrobacterium were positively correlated with MR, but the soil core bacteria, including Alphaproteobacteria_unclassified, Rhodoplanes, Vicinamibacteraceae_unclassified, and Pedomicrobium, were negatively correlated with MR (Figure 3a, b, and i).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis data shown in Figure 3i.

claim: The leaf core fungal genera Didymella, Pleosporales_unclassified, Subplenodomus, and Bulleromyces were positively correlated with MR.
source: The leaf core fungal genera Didymella, Pleosporales_unclassified, Subplenodomus, and Bulleromyces were positively correlated with MR, but the soil core fungal genera Mortierella, Hypocrea, Pochonia, and Volutella were negatively correlated with MR (Figure 3e, f, and j).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis data shown in Figure 3j.

claim: The soil core fungal genera Mortierella, Hypocrea, Pochonia, and Volutella were negatively correlated with MR.
source: The leaf core fungal genera Didymella, Pleosporales_unclassified, Subplenodomus, and Bulleromyces were positively correlated with MR, but the soil core fungal genera Mortierella, Hypocrea, Pochonia, and Volutella were negatively correlated with MR (Figure 3e, f, and j).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis data shown in Figure 3j.

claim: 192 cultivable fungal isolates were obtained from 40 dead seedlings, with an average of 4.825 isolates per dead seedling.
source: We obtained 192 cultivable fungal isolates from 40 dead seedlings, with an average of 4.825 isolates per dead seedling (Figure 4a).
evidence: The claim is supported by isolation data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: The cultivable fungal isolates were divided into seven families based on the ITS genes of the representative strains.
source: Based on the ITS genes of the representative strains (Figure 4—source data 1), they were divided into seven families.
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis based on ITS gene sequences.

claim: The dominant family was Didymellaceae (relative abundance = 66.15%).
source: The dominant family was Didymellaceae (relative abundance = 66.15%), and the numerically dominant genera were Allophoma (50.52%), Alternaria (26.04%), and Epicoccum (5.73%) (Figure 4b, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by taxonomic composition data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: The numerically dominant genera were Allophoma (50.52%), Alternaria (26.04%), and Epicoccum (5.73%).
source: The dominant family was Didymellaceae (relative abundance = 66.15%), and the numerically dominant genera were Allophoma (50.52%), Alternaria (26.04%), and Epicoccum (5.73%) (Figure 4b, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by taxonomic composition data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: The seedling-killing effects of fungal strains on A. adenophora exhibited a significant phylogenetic signal (Pagel's λ=0.82, p=0.0002).
source: The seedling-killing effects of these strains on A. adenophora exhibited a significant phylogenetic signal (Pagel's λ=0.82, p=0.0002).
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic signal analysis with Pagel's λ test showing statistical significance.

claim: Numerically dominant Allophoma (Didymellaceae) and Alternaria (Pleosporaceae) had high seedling mortality (54–100%).
source: Overall, numerically dominant Allophoma (Didymellaceae) and Alternaria (Pleosporaceae) had high seedling mortality (54–100%) (Figure 4c, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by seedling mortality data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: All four factors significantly affected the bacterial community and functional assembly of the seedlings.
source: Nonmetric multidimensional scaling (NMDS) and permutational analysis of variance (PERMANOVA) revealed that all four factors significantly affected the bacterial community and functional assembly of the seedlings, and the greatest effects were inoculation time and compartment (all p<0.05, R2: 0.102–0.138), followed by inoculation source and nutrition (all p<0.05, R2: 0.024–0.082, Figure 5a, b, e, and f).
evidence: The claim is supported by PERMANOVA analysis results shown in Figure 5a, b, e, and f with statistical significance.

claim: The greatest effects on bacterial community and functional assembly were inoculation time and compartment (all p<0.05, R2: 0.102–0.138).
source: Nonmetric multidimensional scaling (NMDS) and permutational analysis of variance (PERMANOVA) revealed that all four factors significantly affected the bacterial community and functional assembly of the seedlings, and the greatest effects were inoculation time and compartment (all p<0.05, R2: 0.102–0.138), followed by inoculation source and nutrition (all p<0.05, R2: 0.024–0.082, Figure 5a, b, e, and f).
evidence: The claim is supported by PERMANOVA analysis results showing R2 values and statistical significance.

claim: Compartment, inoculation source, and time significantly affected the fungal community and functional assembly.
source: Additionally, compartment, inoculation source, and time significantly affected the fungal community and functional assembly (all p<0.05, R2: 0.054–0.102), but nutrition affected only the fungal community (p=0.001, R2=0.031) (Figure 5c, d, g, and h).
evidence: The claim is supported by PERMANOVA analysis results shown in Figure 5c, d, g, and h with statistical significance.

claim: Nutrition affected only the fungal community (p=0.001, R2=0.031).
source: Additionally, compartment, inoculation source, and time significantly affected the fungal community and functional assembly (all p<0.05, R2: 0.054–0.102), but nutrition affected only the fungal community (p=0.001, R2=0.031) (Figure 5c, d, g, and h).
evidence: The claim is supported by PERMANOVA analysis results showing nutrition only affected fungal community but not functional assembly.

claim: Compartment and inoculation source mainly affected the microbial community and functional assembly and explained a greater proportion of the variation in bacteria than in fungi and in function than in the community.
source: Further analysis for each inoculation time treatment showed that compartment and inoculation source mainly affected the microbial community and functional assembly and explained a greater proportion of the variation in bacteria than in fungi and in function than in the community.
evidence: The claim is supported by further PERMANOVA analysis comparing the effects on bacteria vs fungi and community vs function.

claim: The nutrient level mainly affected the bacterial community at certain inoculation time (p<0.05 for G0, G21, and G28).
source: The nutrient level mainly affected the bacterial community at certain inoculation time (p<0.05 for G0, G21, and G28, Figure 5i–l, Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Figure 5—source data 1 and 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by PERMANOVA analysis results shown in Figure 5i-l with statistical significance at specific timepoints.

claim: 47 root endophytic genera were significantly correlated with A. adenophora growth.
source: We identified 47 root endophytic genera that were significantly correlated with A. adenophora growth.
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis between root endophytic genera and seedling growth response index.

claim: Seven negative genera were less abundant in seedlings treated by leaf inoculation than in those treated by soil inoculation.
source: Among these genera, seven negative genera were less abundant in seedlings treated by leaf inoculation than in those treated by soil inoculation but were similar in abundance in seedlings treated by different inoculation time, and in seedlings grown at different nutrient levels.
evidence: The claim is supported by abundance comparison data across different treatments.

claim: 40 positive genera were more abundant in seedlings treated by leaf inoculation than by soil inoculation but less abundant in seedlings inoculated at G0 than at the other three inoculation time treatments.
source: In contrast, 40 positive genera, e.g., the fungi Duganella and Mortierella and the bacteria Massilia, Pseudomonas, and Sphingomonas, were more abundant in seedlings treated by leaf inoculation than by soil inoculation but less abundant in seedlings inoculated at G0 than at the other three inoculation time treatments (Figure 6a).
evidence: The claim is supported by abundance comparison data shown in Figure 6a.

claim: 18 leaf endophytic genera with significant correlations with the RI were identified.
source: Eighteen leaf endophytic genera with significant correlations with the RI were identified, of which three negative genera, namely, the bacteria Tardiphaga and Brevundimonas and the fungus Microsphaera, were more abundant in seedlings inoculated at G0 than at the other three inoculation time treatments and were slightly more abundant in the seedlings inoculated with soil than in those inoculated with leaf
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis between leaf endophytic genera and seedling growth response index.

claim: Three negative leaf endophytic genera (Tardiphaga, Brevundimonas, and Microsphaera) were more abundant in seedlings inoculated at G0 than at the other three inoculation time treatments.
source: Eighteen leaf endophytic genera with significant correlations with the RI were identified, of which three negative genera, namely, the bacteria Tardiphaga and Brevundimonas and the fungus Microsphaera, were more abundant in seedlings inoculated at G0 than at the other three inoculation time treatments and were slightly more abundant in the seedlings inoculated with soil than in those inoculated with leaf
evidence: The claim is supported by abundance comparison data across different inoculation timepoints.

claim: 15 positive leaf endophytic genera were more abundant in the seedlings inoculated with leaf than in those inoculated with soil and were more abundant in the seedlings inoculated at G21 than in the seedlings inoculated at the other three inoculation time treatments.
source: in contrast, 15 positive genera, e.g., the fungi Hypocrea and Pleosporales_unclassified, were more abundant in the seedlings inoculated with leaf than in those inoculated with soil and were more abundant in the seedlings inoculated at G21 than in the seedlings inoculated at the other three inoculation time treatments (Figure 6b).
evidence: The claim is supported by abundance comparison data shown in Figure 6b.

claim: Two bacterial functions involved in the N cycle (nitrate ammonification and nitrite ammonification) in roots showed a significant positive correlation with RI.
source: Two bacterial functions involved in the N cycle (nitrate ammonification and nitrite ammonification) in roots showed a significant positive correlation with RI (Figure 6c).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis data shown in Figure 6c.

claim: The fungal guild Ectomycorrhizal showed a significantly positive correlation with seedling growth.
source: The fungal guild Ectomycorrhizal showed a significantly positive correlation.
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis between fungal guilds and seedling growth response index.

claim: The putative plant pathogen guild showed a significant positive correlation with seedling growth.
source: Unexpectedly, the putative plant pathogen guild showed a significant positive correlation with seedling growth, while the arbuscular mycorrhizal guild showed a negative correlation (Figure 6d and e).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis data shown in Figure 6d and e.

claim: The arbuscular mycorrhizal guild showed a negative correlation with seedling growth.
source: Unexpectedly, the putative plant pathogen guild showed a significant positive correlation with seedling growth, while the arbuscular mycorrhizal guild showed a negative correlation (Figure 6d and e).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis data shown in Figure 6d and e.

claim: The positive bacterial functions in roots and fungal guilds in leaves had greater relative abundances in the seedlings after leaf inoculation than those after soil inoculation.
source: The positive bacterial functions in roots and fungal guilds in leaves had greater relative abundances in the seedlings after leaf inoculation than those after soil inoculation (Figure 6c and e)
evidence: The claim is supported by abundance comparison data shown in Figure 6c and e.

claim: The positive fungal guilds in roots and leaves had significantly greater abundances in the G21 seedlings than in those at the other three inoculation time treatments.
source: additionally, the positive fungal guilds in roots and leaves had significantly greater abundances in the G21 seedlings than in those at the other three inoculation time treatments.
evidence: The claim is supported by abundance comparison data across different inoculation timepoints.

claim: There was no difference in the relative abundance of microbes or functions involved in seedling growth under different nutrient levels.
source: Surprisingly, there was no difference in the relative abundance of microbes or functions involved in seedling growth under different nutrient levels (Figure 6a–e).
evidence: The claim is supported by abundance comparison data shown in Figure 6a-e showing no significant differences between nutrient levels.

claim: Leaf litter possibly produces allelochemicals that adversely impact A. adenophora seed GT and seedling survival.
source: Our study did not directly test the allelopathic effects of leaf litter. However, leaf litter possibly produces allelochemicals that adversely impact A. adenophora seed GT and seedling survival.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that sterile leaf litter caused longer germination times and seedling mortality, suggesting chemical rather than microbial effects.

claim: Some pathways through which leaf microbes alleviate the adverse effects of leaf allelopathy on GTs are unknown.
source: Interestingly, sterile leaf litter inoculation also caused longer GTs than non-sterile leaf litter inoculation, suggesting that some pathways through which leaf microbes alleviate the adverse effects of leaf allelopathy on GTs are unknown.
evidence: The claim is based on the observation that non-sterile leaves caused shorter germination times than sterile leaves, suggesting microbial amelioration of chemical effects.

claim: Self-limiting of the population elicited by leaf microbes may alleviate intraspecific competition thus in turn help to maintain monocultures at old established sites.
source: For those perennial invasive species, e.g., A. adenophora, self-limiting of the population elicited by leaf microbes may alleviate intraspecific competition thus in turn help to maintain monocultures at old established sites.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation about the ecological role of leaf microbe-mediated seedling mortality in maintaining established populations.

claim: Small seedlings usually allocate most of their resources to survive and grow, while older seedlings have relatively more resources to defend against pathogen infection.
source: One potential reason is that small seedlings usually allocate most of their resources to survive and grow, while older seedlings have relatively more resources to defend against pathogen infection (Geisen et al., 2021; Schloter and Matyssek, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research (Geisen et al., 2021; Schloter and Matyssek, 2009).

claim: Smaller seedlings were more sensitive to inoculated individual fungi, soil microbiota, or litter addition than older seedlings due to fewer defense resources and little chance of recovering from biomass loss.
source: For example, smaller seedlings were more sensitive to inoculated individual fungi, soil microbiota, or litter addition than older seedlings due to fewer defense resources and little chance of recovering from biomass loss (Geisen et al., 2021; Jevon et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research (Geisen et al., 2021; Jevon et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2022).

claim: Seed-borne endophytes are likely to be beneficial for seedling growth and stress resistance.
source: There is evidence that seed-borne endophytes are likely to be beneficial for seedling growth and stress resistance (Díaz Herrera et al., 2016; Wang and Zhang, 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research (Díaz Herrera et al., 2016; Wang and Zhang, 2023).

claim: Seed endophytes might be inhibited or even excluded from young seedlings by external sources of microbes inoculated at G0.
source: These seed endophytes might be inhibited or even excluded from young seedlings by external sources of microbes inoculated at G0, when seedlings are highly sensitive to inoculated microbes (Geisen et al., 2021; Jevon et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that early inoculation has more adverse effects, possibly due to interference with beneficial seed endophytes.

claim: A. adenophora invasion increased N circle-related bacterial functional genes in soil and subsequently directly promoted plant growth and invasion.
source: Similarly, Zhao et al., 2019, showed that A. adenophora invasion increased N circle-related bacterial functional genes in soil and subsequently directly promoted plant growth and invasion.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Zhao et al., 2019.

claim: Several root endophytic nitrogen-ﬁxing bacteria of A. adenophora could significantly promote its growth.
source: Fang et al., 2019b, also reported that several root endophytic nitrogen-ﬁxing bacteria of A. adenophora could significantly promote its growth.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Fang et al., 2019b.

claim: Some N circle-related bacteria associated with leaf litter may migrate from leaves into roots after leaf litter inoculation.
source: Interestingly, the abundance of these N circle-related bacterial functions was greater in seedling roots inoculated with leaf litter than in those inoculated with soil (Figure 6c), which suggests a possible way in which some N circle-related bacteria associated with leaf litter may migrate from leaves into roots after leaf litter inoculation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that N cycle-related functions were more abundant in roots after leaf inoculation, suggesting bacterial migration from leaves to roots.

claim: Invasive plants often have greater nutrient availability than do native plants.
source: Nutrient addition can promote severe invasion, as invasive plants often have greater nutrient availability than do native plants (Shan et al., 2024; Slate et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research (Shan et al., 2024; Slate et al., 2022).

claim: A. adenophora grew larger and more rapidly in the high nutrient treatment than in the low nutrient treatment.
source: We also found that A. adenophora grew larger and more rapidly in the high nutrient treatment than in the low nutrient treatment (Figure 7—figure supplement 2)
evidence: The claim is supported by growth data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: The nutrient level significantly changed the microbial community and bacterial function.
source: moreover, the nutrient level significantly changed the microbial community and bacterial function (Figure 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by PERMANOVA analysis results shown in Figure 5.

claim: The invasion advantage driven by high nutrient availability may be driven primarily by plant physiological traits, such as rapid nutrient absorption and growth strategies, rather than by enriched microbes.
source: Our data indicated that the invasion advantage driven by high nutrient availability may be driven primarily by plant physiological traits, such as rapid nutrient absorption and growth strategies, rather than by enriched microbes.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that nutrient levels did not affect microbe-mediated growth effects, suggesting physiological rather than microbial mechanisms.

claim: A high nutrient level resulted in a more significant positive microbial effect on seedling growth than a low nutrient level when inoculated at G21.
source: For example, a high nutrient level resulted in a more significant positive microbial effect on seedling growth than a low nutrient level when inoculated at G21, regardless of leaf litter or soil inoculation.
evidence: The claim is supported by the interaction effect data shown in Figure 2.

claim: During the first 21 days before inoculation, more beneficial seed endophytes may be enriched to produce a more positive effect on seedling growth under high nutrition conditions than under low nutrition conditions.
source: It is unclear whether, during the first 21 days before inoculation, more beneficial seed endophytes are enriched to produce a more positive effect on seedling growth under high nutrition conditions than under low nutrition conditions, as seed endophytes can facilitate nutrient acquisition and subsequently promote plant growth (Khalaf and Raizada, 2016; Sánchez-López et al., 2018; Shao et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the possibility that seed endophytes respond to nutrient conditions, supported by citations about seed endophyte functions.

claim: Seed endophytes can facilitate nutrient acquisition and subsequently promote plant growth.
source: It is unclear whether, during the first 21 days before inoculation, more beneficial seed endophytes are enriched to produce a more positive effect on seedling growth under high nutrition conditions than under low nutrition conditions, as seed endophytes can facilitate nutrient acquisition and subsequently promote plant growth (Khalaf and Raizada, 2016; Sánchez-López et al., 2018; Shao et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research (Khalaf and Raizada, 2016; Sánchez-López et al., 2018; Shao et al., 2021).

claim: Many strains belonging to Pseudomonas, Sphingomonas, and Massilia have been reported to promote the growth of many plant species.
source: For example, the bacterial genera Pseudomonas, Sphingomonas, and Massilia are positively correlated with seedling mortality and subsequent seedling growth (Figures 3 and 6). Many strains belonging to these genera have been reported to promote the growth of many plant species (Jiménez et al., 2020; Luo et al., 2019; Qiao et al., 2019), including A. adenophora (Chen et al., 2019; Fang et al., 2019a), because they are commonly involved in N2 fixation (Albino et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research (Jiménez et al., 2020; Luo et al., 2019; Qiao et al., 2019).

claim: Strains of Pseudomonas, Sphingomonas, and Massilia have been reported to promote A. adenophora growth.
source: Many strains belonging to these genera have been reported to promote the growth of many plant species (Jiménez et al., 2020; Luo et al., 2019; Qiao et al., 2019), including A. adenophora (Chen et al., 2019; Fang et al., 2019a), because they are commonly involved in N2 fixation (Albino et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research (Chen et al., 2019; Fang et al., 2019a).

claim: Pseudomonas, Sphingomonas, and Massilia are commonly involved in N2 fixation.
source: Many strains belonging to these genera have been reported to promote the growth of many plant species (Jiménez et al., 2020; Luo et al., 2019; Qiao et al., 2019), including A. adenophora (Chen et al., 2019; Fang et al., 2019a), because they are commonly involved in N2 fixation (Albino et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Albino et al., 2006.

claim: Mortierella and Hypocrea are plant growth-promoting fungi that have been widely reported.
source: However, some microbes, e.g., the fungi Mortierella and Hypocrea, are negatively correlated with early seedling mortality but positively correlated with later seedling growth (Figures 3 and 6). These fungi, as plant growth-promoting fungi, have been widely reported (Contreras-Cornejo et al., 2009; Ozimek and Hanaka, 2024; Wani et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research (Contreras-Cornejo et al., 2009; Ozimek and Hanaka, 2024; Wani et al., 2017).

claim: The bacteria Massilia, Pseudomonas, and Sphingomonas may negatively affect seedling growth and even kill seedlings if the arrival time is too early after germination.
source: On the one hand, there may be sequential effects for some plant growth-promoting microbial groups. For example, the bacteria Massilia, Pseudomonas, and Sphingomonas may negatively affect seedling growth and even kill seedlings if the arrival time is too early after germination.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that these bacteria are positively correlated with mortality when present early but promote growth later.

claim: Most Pseudomonas and Sphingomonas amplicon sequence variants (ASVs) enriched in the seedlings (>80%) were not associated with the inoculum source.
source: Interestingly, we found that most Pseudomonas and Sphingomonas amplicon sequence variants (ASVs) enriched in the seedlings (>80%) were not associated with the inoculum source (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by ASV analysis data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Most of the bacterial ASVs positively correlated with growth might be from seeds rather than from the inocula.
source: This suggested that most of the bacterial ASVs positively correlated with growth might be from seeds rather than from the inocula.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that most ASVs were not associated with inoculum sources, suggesting seed origin.

claim: Putative plant pathogens were classified as plant pathogens based on the current database.
source: Because these putative plant pathogens were classified as plant pathogens based on the current database, it remains to determine whether such putative plant pathogens for most native plant species are not detrimental to invader A. adenophora growth.
evidence: The claim is based on the methodology of functional guild assignment using databases.

claim: Plant pathogens often can switch from a beneficial endophyte to a pathogen or vice versa depending on different host plant species.
source: Indeed, plant pathogens often can switch from a beneficial endophyte to a pathogen or vice versa depending on different host plant species (Delaye et al., 2013; Tian et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research (Delaye et al., 2013; Tian et al., 2020).

claim: Most seedling-killing microbes isolated from dead seedlings were previously reported to be leaf spot pathogens.
source: We found that most seedling-killing microbes isolated from dead seedlings were previously reported to be leaf spot pathogens.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of isolated strains with previously reported pathogens in the literature.

claim: Alternaria sp. is often pathogenic to a large variety of plants, causing stem cancer, leaf blight, or leaf spot.
source: For example, Alternaria (Pleosporaceae) and several genera belonging to the family Didymellaceae, such as Allophoma, Stagonosporopsis, Didymella, Boeremia, and Epicoccum, caused high seedling mortality (Figure 4). Alternaria sp. is often pathogenic to a large variety of plants, such as those causing stem cancer, leaf blight, or leaf spot (Leiminger et al., 2015; Thomma, 2003; Mercado Vergnes et al., 2006)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research (Leiminger et al., 2015; Thomma, 2003; Mercado Vergnes et al., 2006).

claim: Members of Allophoma have been reported to cause dieback and leaf spot.
source: and members of Allophoma have also been reported to cause dieback (Babaahmadi et al., 2018) and leaf spot (Garibaldi et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research (Babaahmadi et al., 2018; Garibaldi et al., 2012).

claim: All these fungi are leaf spot pathogens of A. adenophora and its neighboring native plant.
source: All these fungi are leaf spot pathogens of A. adenophora and its neighboring native plant (Chen et al., 2022; Fang et al., 2021b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research (Chen et al., 2022; Fang et al., 2021b).

claim: The numerically dominant Allophoma strains obtained in this study had the same ITS genes as the leaf endophyte and leaf spot pathogen Allophoma associated with A. adenophora.
source: In particular, the numerically dominant Allophoma strains obtained in this study had the same ITS genes as the leaf endophyte and leaf spot pathogen Allophoma associated with A. adenophora (Chen et al., 2022; Fang et al., 2021a; Yang et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by ITS gene sequence comparison and citations to previous research (Chen et al., 2022; Fang et al., 2021a; Yang et al., 2023).

claim: The dominant genera in healthy seedlings inoculated with leaf litter were Didymella and Alternaria.
source: Interestingly, a previous report revealed that the dominant genera in healthy seedlings inoculated with leaf litter were Didymella and Alternaria (Fang et al., 2019b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Fang et al., 2019b.

claim: These fungal genera likely exist in A. adenophora mature individual experiencing a lifestyle switch from endophytic to pathogenic and play an essential role in limiting the population density of A. adenophora monocultures by killing seedlings only at very early stages.
source: We could assume that these fungal genera likely exist in A. adenophora mature individual experiencing a lifestyle switch from endophytic to pathogenic and play an essential role in limiting the population density of A. adenophora monocultures by killing seedlings only at very early stages.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the observation that these fungi are present as endophytes in mature plants but kill seedlings.

claim: Several leaf spot fungi have been used as biological agents for the control of plant invasion.
source: Currently, several leaf spot fungi, such as the leaf spot fungus Phaeoramularia sp., which is released against A. adenophora (Kluge, 1991); the white smut fungus Entyloma ageratinae against A. riparia (Barton et al., 2007); the rust fungus Uromycladium tepperianum against the weed Acacia saligna (Wood, 2012); and the rust fungus Puccinia spegazzinii against Mikania micrantha (Day and Riding, 2019), have been used as biological agents for the control of plant invasion.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research (Kluge, 1991; Barton et al., 2007; Wood, 2012; Day and Riding, 2019).

claim: Leaf spot fungal agents mainly control weeds by damaging the leaves, stems, and petioles and reducing growth rates, flowering, percentage cover, and population density.
source: These agents mainly control weeds by damaging the leaves, stems, and petioles and reducing growth rates, flowering, percentage cover, and population density.
evidence: The claim is based on general knowledge about how fungal biocontrol agents work.

claim: Strains associated with leaf litter, such as Allophoma sp. and Alternaria sp., could control A. adenophora invasion at the seedling establishment stage.
source: In this study, the strains associated with leaf litter, such as Allophoma sp. and Alternaria sp., caused high seedling mortality and thus could control A. adenophora invasion at the seedling establishment stage.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that these strains cause high seedling mortality, suggesting potential for biocontrol application.

claim: Prevention and control measures by microbial agents taken at the early seedling stage of invasive plants may be more effective than at the mature stage.
source: On the other hand, we found that an external source of microbes had a greater adverse effect on seedling survival and growth when inoculated at G0 than at the later growth stage. Therefore, prevention and control measures by microbial agents taken at the early seedling stage of invasive plants may be more effective than at the mature stage.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that early-stage seedlings are more susceptible to microbial effects.

claim: Gamma irradiation at 30 kGy for 30 hr can kill all microorganisms.
source: The sterile groups (soils or litter) were sterilized by gamma irradiation (30 kGy, 30 hr, Huayuan Nuclear Radiation Technology Co., Ltd., Kunming, China), which can kill all microorganisms because no colonies were formed after 7 days of inoculation on PDA media for gamma-irradiated samples (see Figure 7—figure supplement 1)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental verification shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1 showing no colony formation.

claim: There was no evidence that gamma irradiation changed the chemistry of the samples.
source: moreover, there was no evidence that this irradiation method changed the chemistry of the samples.
evidence: The claim is based on the absence of observed chemical changes, though no specific chemical analysis data is presented.
